summary: Gives an overview of the NSIS framework and protocol suite created from 2001 to 2010, with suggestions for how industry can use them and how they can be extended for future signaling needs. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: A guidebook that explains the whole set of messenger tools made for the network and how they might be used.

subtitle: A two-layer framework for signaling on the Internet with QoS and NAT traversal support.

tldr.problem: Internet signaling protocols need to support mobility, QoS signaling, and NAT/firewall traversal while being more flexible than RSVP.
tldr.mechanism: NSIS divides signaling into two layers: a generic transport layer (GIST) that discovers signaling peers and manages connections, and protocol-specific signaling layers (NSLPs) for QoS and NAT/firewall tasks.
tldr.outcome: The suite was published as Experimental status in 2010 to gather deployment experience. Its use of Router Alert Options raised security concerns, limiting initial deployment to controlled networks.

today: RFC 5978 is an informational RFC that documents the NSIS framework and protocol suite as they stood in 2010. The protocols are defined in related RFCs with Experimental status. The use of Router Alert Options remains a limiting factor for widespread deployment.

sections.title: Two-Layer Framework
sections.content:
The NSIS (Next Steps in Signaling) framework was developed from 2001 to 2010 as an improved approach to Internet signaling protocols. Unlike RSVP, which tries to do everything in one protocol, NSIS uses a clean two-layer design: a generic signaling transport protocol (GIST) on the bottom, and specific signaling applications (NSLPs) on top. This separation allows the same transport infrastructure to support multiple signaling tasks without being redesigned for each one.

The architecture is designed for path-coupled signaling, where signaling messages follow the same network path as the data they apply to. Each signaling application gets its own NSLP with a unique identifier (NSLPID), and GIST handles the low-level details of finding the next signaling node, choosing appropriate transport protocols, and managing security. A Session Identifier (SID) allows signaling state to be maintained across IP address changes due to mobility.
sections.plainLanguage: Think of NSIS like a mail delivery system. The bottom layer is the postal service itself (GIST), and the top layer is what goes in the envelopes (NSLPs). The postal service just needs to deliver whatever is inside, and different things can be mailed using the same postal system.

sections.title: General Internet Signaling Transport (GIST)
sections.content:
GIST provides the signaling transport foundation by discovering the next-hop signaling peer using a Query message that carries the NSLP identifier and Message Routing Information (MRI). When a peer receives this query and decides to participate, GIST establishes a Message Routing State (MRS) between them through a three-way handshake that includes security protections like cookie mechanisms against denial-of-service attacks.

GIST can use existing protocols like UDP for unreliable signaling, TCP for reliable signaling, and TLS over TCP for secure signaling. It reuses Messaging Associations (MAs) across multiple flows when their transport requirements are compatible, reducing overhead. Soft-state management means all state expires automatically unless refreshed, similar to RSVP. GIST also detects routing changes and notifies NSLPs so they can update their state as needed.

A critical challenge GIST faced is the use of the Router Alert Option (RAO) in IPv4 and IPv6 to ensure intermediate nodes intercept signaling packets. Late in development, serious concerns emerged about RAO's security risks (enabling denial-of-service attacks on router control planes) and about incompatible router implementations. These concerns led to the NSIS protocol suite being published as Experimental rather than Standards Track, pending deployment experience.
sections.plainLanguage: GIST is like the post office finding the right address and choosing whether to use regular mail (UDP), registered mail (TCP), or certified mail with a signature (TLS). It remembers which post offices it talks to and stops remembering if they go quiet.

sections.title: Quality-of-Service and NAT/Firewall Signaling
sections.content:
The QoS NSLP allows applications to request resources from the network for data flows, similar in concept to RSVP but with important improvements. It supports both sender-initiated and receiver-initiated reservations, bidirectional reservations, and edge-to-edge signaling. Resource requirements are expressed using QSPECs (QoS Specifications), which are separate from the signaling protocol itself, allowing different QoS models (like Diffserv) to be used with the same signaling protocol.

The NAT/firewall traversal NSLP addresses the challenge of dynamic firewall configuration, allowing hosts to request that firewalls open pinholes or NATs translate addresses on demand. It lets end-hosts authorize the creation of (pattern, action) rules where patterns match packet headers and actions are allow or deny. This enables firewall-protected hosts to participate in applications that require inbound connectivity, and it supports a proxy mode for hosts that cannot run NSIS themselves.
sections.plainLanguage: The QoS tool is like telling the network 'I need a fast lane for video.' The firewall tool is like calling ahead to say 'please let this traffic through when it arrives.'

sections.title: Deployment and Extensibility
sections.content:
NSIS is designed for incremental deployment: not every router needs to support it, and proxy modes allow unsophisticated hosts to benefit from NSIS without implementing it. However, several practical deployment obstacles exist. Router Alert Option handling is inconsistent across implementations, many firewalls and NATs filter packets with IP options as a security practice, and some routers drop RAO-marked UDP packets because they lack dedicated handlers.

The protocol suite is highly extensible at multiple levels. New Message Routing Methods (MRMs) can be defined for different signaling scenarios. GIST can use different transport protocols (proposals exist for DCCP and SCTP with DTLS security). NSLPs can define new signaling applications using the same GIST infrastructure, and new objects with extensibility flags (A/B flags) can be carried in messages without breaking existing implementations. QoS models can be defined by creating new QSPEC specifications. This extensibility allows NSIS to adapt to future signaling needs without rebuilding the entire framework.
sections.plainLanguage: Deployment is like getting every post office to handle a new service: some will do it right away, others later, and some may need workarounds. New types of mail (new NSLPs) can be added as long as the postal system (GIST) can handle them.

sections.title: Security and Standardization Status
sections.content:
Basic security functions are provided at the GIST layer, including protection against blind denial-of-service attacks and cookie-based state installation. Transport security can be provided by TLS between signaling peers for authentication and confidentiality. However, the use of Router Alert Options introduces potential attack vectors for distributed denial-of-service attacks on router control planes, which led service providers to restrict host-to-router signaling in customer networks.

The NSIS framework was published with Experimental status rather than as an Internet Standard. This decision reflects the security concerns with RAO, implementation challenges across router vendors, and the need to gain operational experience before committing to Standards Track. Further authorization mechanisms continue to be developed to allow per-user and per-service authorization in signaling protocols. Any extensions to NSIS must carefully assess security implications and provide means to authenticate messages and control resource allocation.
sections.plainLanguage: Security is a big concern: we need to trust the postal workers and make sure bad actors cannot flood the system by pretending to send lots of mail. The experimental status means 'let's try this in controlled environments first.'
